Two arms or jaws that come together from opposite sides to grip, trap, or squeeze something in the middle.

That's the soul of "pincer." Every meaning this word carries is a variation of that same idea.

A pincer (most often used in the plural — pincers) is a handheld tool made of two arms joined at a pivot, similar in shape to a pair of scissors. But unlike scissors, which are meant to cut, pincers are meant to grip and pull.

You squeeze the two arms together with your hand, and the jaws at the other end close around an object — a nail, a wire, a small component — so you can pull it out or hold it in place.

Think of it as a more powerful, more precise version of your own fingers pinching something. The tool does what your fingers can't — it grips harder, reaches into tight spaces, and holds with more control.

Everyday example: A carpenter uses pincers to pull a bent nail out of a piece of wood. A jeweller uses them to hold a tiny gem while setting it into a ring.

Related tools you might know: Pincers belong to a family of gripping tools that includes pliers, tongs, and tweezers. The differences are subtle (pliers are more general-purpose, pincers are typically designed for pulling), but they all share that same two-jaw gripping action.

When you look at a crab, lobster, scorpion, or beetle, you'll notice that some of their limbs end in a claw-like structure — two parts that open and snap shut. That structure is called a pincer (also called a claw or, in biology, a chela).

Functionally, it's identical to the tool: two opposing parts that come together to grip. Animals use their pincers to catch food, defend themselves, crush shells, or grip surfaces.

Example: A lobster raises its pincers when it feels threatened, ready to snap them shut on anything that comes close. A scorpion uses the pincers at the front of its body (near its mouth) to grab prey and hold it steady while stinging it.

Notice that the scorpion actually has two sets of "pincer-like" structures — the claws near its head, and the curved stinger at the tip of its tail. When people say "scorpion pincers," they typically mean the front claws.

This meaning steps away from physical objects and into strategy.

In warfare, a pincer (or pincer movement) is a tactical manoeuvre where two forces attack an enemy from two opposite sides at the same time, trapping the enemy in the middle — just like the two jaws of a pincer tool closing around something.

The goal is to surround the enemy, cut off their ability to retreat or receive reinforcements, and force them to fight on two fronts simultaneously — which is extremely difficult to do.

Example: If one army is positioned in a valley, and two enemy forces advance from the left and from the right at the same time, that's a pincer movement. The army in the middle is squeezed, just like a nail being pulled by pincers.

This is one of the oldest and most powerful tactics in military history. It has been used for thousands of years, from ancient battles to World War II.
Singular vs. plural — a small but important note

• When referring to the tool, you almost always use the plural: "a pair of pincers" or simply "pincers." Saying "a pincer" for the tool sounds slightly unusual, though it's not wrong.
  • When referring to animal claws, both "a pincer" (singular, one claw) and "pincers" (both claws together) are natural and common.
  • When referring to the military tactic, you say "a pincer movement" or "a pincer attack" — here "pincer" is used as a singular modifier before a noun.
The thread that ties it all together

No matter which meaning you encounter, a pincer always involves two opposing parts converging on a target from both sides — to grip it, trap it, or overwhelm it. If you remember that image, you'll immediately understand "pincer" in any context you come across it.
